<warm> The danger zone. <short pause> Time and temperature control.

<friendly> Welcome back to Kitchen Fundamentals. <short pause> This is part two of our ten-part series.

<serious> Here's the short version. <short pause> Keep cold food at forty degrees Fahrenheit, that's four Celsius, or below. Keep hot food at one hundred forty Fahrenheit, sixty Celsius, or above. <short pause> Food left in between for more than two hours goes in the bin. And if it's hotter than ninety Fahrenheit, thirty-two Celsius, you only get one hour. <short pause> Cook to safe internal temperatures, measured with a thermometer. Cool leftovers quickly. And reheat them to one sixty-five Fahrenheit, seventy-four Celsius.

<long pause> <curious> So, what exactly is the danger zone?

It's the temperature range from roughly forty to one hundred forty degrees Fahrenheit. <short pause> Four to sixty, in Celsius. Inside that range, many bacteria can double in about twenty minutes.

<quietly> A few hundred cells on a chicken salad at lunchtime... <short pause> can become millions by dinner.

<serious> And here's the part people miss. <short pause> Some bacteria also produce toxins that cooking does not destroy. <short pause> That's why reheating spoiled food does not make it safe.

<long pause> <friendly> Next, the two-hour rule.

Perishable food should spend no more than two hours in the danger zone, in total. <short pause> Shopping, prep, serving, and leftovers, they all count.

If the room or the weather is above ninety degrees Fahrenheit, thirty-two Celsius, the limit drops to one hour.

<warm> And when in doubt, throw it out. <short pause> Smell and appearance are not reliable tests.

<long pause> <friendly> Let's talk about keeping things cold.

Your refrigerator should be at forty degrees Fahrenheit, four Celsius, or below. <short pause> Around thirty-seven Fahrenheit, three Celsius, gives you a nice margin.

Your freezer should be at zero Fahrenheit, minus eighteen Celsius. <short pause> And remember, freezing pauses bacteria. <short pause> It does not kill them.

Keep an inexpensive appliance thermometer in both. <chuckles> Built-in dials are often wrong.

<long pause> <friendly> Now, keeping things hot.

Food kept warm for serving should stay at one hundred forty degrees Fahrenheit, sixty Celsius, or above. <short pause> A slow cooker on warm, a low oven, or a chafing dish all work.

<lighthearted> Lukewarm buffets? <short pause> That's where trouble starts.

<long pause> <serious> Next, safe internal temperatures. <short pause> And here's the golden rule: color is not a doneness test.

Use an instant-read thermometer in the thickest part of the food, away from the bone.

Poultry, whole or ground, and stuffing, one sixty-five Fahrenheit, seventy-four Celsius.

Ground beef, pork, lamb and veal, one sixty Fahrenheit, seventy-one Celsius.

Whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb and veal, one forty-five Fahrenheit, sixty-three Celsius, and then let them rest for three minutes.

Fish and shellfish, one forty-five Fahrenheit, sixty-three Celsius, or until the flesh is opaque and flakes apart.

Egg dishes, one sixty Fahrenheit, seventy-one Celsius.

And leftovers and casseroles, one sixty-five Fahrenheit, seventy-four Celsius.

<short pause> <friendly> One handy trick. Check your thermometer now and then in a glass of ice water, stirred for a minute. <short pause> It should read thirty-two Fahrenheit, zero Celsius.

<long pause> <curious> What about cooling leftovers?

A big pot of hot stew cools slowly in the middle. <short pause> It can sit in the danger zone for hours, even inside the fridge.

So, divide it into shallow containers, so the food is no deeper than about two inches, five centimeters. <short pause> Cut large roasts into smaller pieces. <short pause> Stir over an ice bath to speed things up.

Refrigerate within two hours of cooking. <short pause> Leave the lids slightly open until the food is cold, and then seal them.

<quietly> The professional standard? <short pause> From one thirty-five to seventy Fahrenheit, that's fifty-seven to twenty-one Celsius, within two hours. <short pause> Then down to forty-one Fahrenheit, five Celsius, within four more.

<long pause> <friendly> Now, reheating.

Reheat leftovers to one sixty-five Fahrenheit, seventy-four Celsius, all the way through. <short pause> Bring sauces, soups and gravies to a rolling boil.

In a microwave, cover the food, stir halfway, and let it stand before checking the temperature. <short pause> <playful> Microwaves love to leave cold spots.

<long pause> <serious> A word about who needs extra care.

Pregnant people, babies and young children, older adults, and anyone with a weakened immune system are more likely to become seriously ill. <short pause> For them, be strict about unpasteurized milk and juice, undercooked eggs and meat, raw sprouts, and deli meats that have not been reheated until steaming.

<long pause> <reflective> Why does this outlast any technology?

Smart fridges and probe thermometers will keep improving. <short pause> But the biology of bacterial growth will not.

<warm> Understand the zone, and you can judge any situation, a power cut, a picnic, a potluck, without an app.
